answer.line: Cl brings 7 valence electrons, spends 3 on the Cl-F bonds, and keeps 4 as two lone pairs.

steps: Count the central atom first. Cl is in group 17, so it brings 7 valence electrons.
Spend them on bonds: three Cl-F single bonds use 3 of the 7, leaving 4.
Pair them up: 4 electrons make 2 lone pairs. Three bonds plus two pairs is five domains, with the pairs equatorial: a T.

choices.note: With no lone pairs ClF3 would be a flat triangle, like BF3. Cl has 4 electrons left after bonding.
One lone pair goes with the seesaw of SF4, or the pyramid of NH3. A T shape takes two.
Three lone pairs sit on each F, or on Xe in linear XeF2. The stem asks about the central Cl.
4 is the leftover electron count. Two electrons make one pair, so 4 electrons are 2 pairs.

lockIt: Lone pairs on the center = (its valence electrons - one per bond) / 2.
hook: Three bonds plus two pairs: T-shaped.

playWith.label: VSEPR Predictor: set 3 bonded atoms and 2 lone pairs and read the T shape

visual.reuse: Copy of the Lewis sandbox layout and drawing functions (tools/gc/lewis-sandbox.html), with the T drawn as F left, right and below and both pairs above
visual.alt: Lewis structure of ClF3: chlorine in the center with single bonds to fluorines on the left, right and below, each fluorine holding three lone pairs, and two outlined lone pairs on chlorine above. A ledger reads 7 valence electrons, 3 in bonds, 4 left over, 2 lone pairs, 5 domains.
visual.caption: The two outlined pairs are the answer. With three bonds they make five domains, which bends ClF3 into a T.
